subject: ela
description: Students determine a theme or central idea of a literary text and analyze how that theme is conveyed through particular details such as characters' choices, dialogue, conflict, setting, and how events resolve. They distinguish a theme (a broad lesson or message about life) from a topic (a one-word subject) and from a plot summary. They also write or select an objective summary of the text that captures the key events and ideas in sequence while leaving out personal opinions, judgments, and reactions. Every item embeds the full passage, poem, or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer it.
subSkills: Distinguish a theme (a message or lesson about life) from a topic (a one-word subject such as friendship or courage)
Determine the theme or central idea of a literary text using evidence from the whole passage
Identify the specific details (character actions, dialogue, conflict, turning points, resolution) that convey or develop the theme
Explain how a chosen detail supports or reveals the theme
Distinguish an objective summary from a personal opinion, judgment, or reaction
Write or select an accurate, objective summary that includes the key events and ideas in order and excludes personal commentary

problemArchetypes.name: Determine the theme
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short fable, then answer: Which statement best expresses the theme of the passage? Answer choices offer one true theme (a life lesson the events teach) plus distractors that are topics, plot restatements, or unsupported claims.

problemArchetypes.name: Theme versus topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. One answer names a topic (such as 'jealousy') and another states a theme (such as 'Jealousy can blind a person to a friend's loyalty'). The student selects the option that is a theme rather than a topic.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the detail that conveys the theme
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. The student is told the theme and must choose which specific detail (a particular action, line of dialogue, or event) best develops or reveals that theme.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how the theme is conveyed
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then explain how the writer conveys the theme through a particular detail, naming the detail and connecting it to the message about life.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the objective summary
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. Several candidate summaries are given; one is accurate and objective, others insert opinions ('the boy was foolish'), omit key events, or add details not in the text. The student selects the objective summary.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the opinion in a summary
problemArchetypes.example: Read a passage and a draft summary. The student identifies which sentence or phrase in the summary is a personal opinion or judgment rather than an objective statement of what happened.

Easy.description: A short, single-event narrative, fable, or poem (roughly 60 to 120 words) with an explicit, easily inferred lesson embedded in the item. The task is to identify the stated or strongly signaled theme, distinguish a theme from a topic, or pick the obvious objective summary. One concept is tested and the supporting detail is direct.
constraints: Stimulus is a 60 to 120 word passage or short poem included in the prompt
Theme is clear and reinforced by a single obvious detail or a closing moral
Identify-level task: select the theme, the topic-versus-theme choice, or the matching objective summary
Distractors are surface-level (a topic word, a single restated event) and easy to rule out
Minimal inference; the lesson is nearly stated in the text

Medium.description: A multi-paragraph excerpt or a complete short scene (roughly 150 to 250 words) with a theme that must be inferred from how events and characters develop. The task requires analysis: connecting a particular detail to the theme, or building or selecting an objective summary that orders the key events and strips out opinion.
constraints: Stimulus is a 150 to 250 word excerpt or short scene included in the prompt
Theme is implied through character choices, conflict, or change over the passage, not stated outright
Analyze-level task: match a theme-revealing detail, or choose the summary that is both complete and objective
Distractors include a plausible-but-too-narrow theme, a summary missing a key event, and a summary containing one opinion
Moderate inference across more than one part of the text

Hard.description: A longer or more complex literary passage (roughly 280 to 400 words) with figurative language, a subtle or layered theme, or a shift in the character's understanding. The task requires evaluation: judging which statement most fully captures the central idea, explaining how a specific detail conveys the theme, or distinguishing a strong objective summary from one that subtly inserts judgment or misorders events.
constraints: Stimulus is a 280 to 400 word passage included in the prompt, possibly with figurative or descriptive language
Theme is subtle, layered, or develops through a change in the character; competing reasonable readings exist
Evaluate-level task: select the best full statement of theme and justify with a detail, or pick the truly objective and complete summary
Distractors are sophisticated: a partially true theme that ignores the resolution, a summary that buries an opinion in objective wording, a summary that reorders or overweights one event
Requires inference across the whole passage and attention to how meaning is built

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the topic with the theme, naming a one-word subject instead of a full message about life
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'friendship' or 'courage' as the theme instead of a complete statement such as 'True friendship means standing by someone even when it is hard'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student restates the plot and calls it the theme, reporting what happened rather than the lesson it teaches
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'A boy lost his dog and then found it' as the theme instead of the message the events convey, such as 'Patience and hope can be rewarded'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a theme that is too narrow or applies only to one character, not the broader message of the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Maya should not have lied to her coach' instead of the generalizable theme 'Dishonesty often costs more than the truth would have'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student chooses a detail that is vivid or memorable but does not actually support the stated theme
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a colorful setting description or a minor event as the theme-conveying detail instead of the character's decisive choice that reveals the lesson

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student includes personal opinions or judgments in a summary, treating reactions as part of what happened
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a summary containing 'the brother was selfish and annoying' or 'this was a sad story' instead of an objective account of the events

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student writes a summary that omits a key event or adds details not in the text, so it is inaccurate even if opinion-free
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a summary that leaves out the turning point, or one that invents a detail the passage never states, instead of the accurate, complete summary

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the first or last sentence as automatically the summary, mistaking a single line for the whole text's key ideas
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a one-sentence quotation or the opening line as the summary instead of a statement that captures the key events and central idea of the full passage
